## Welcome to R Programming! 🚀

This interactive guide will help you learn R from the ground up. You can run all code examples directly in your browser - just click the "Run Code" button in each code block!

### Before We Start: Understanding the R Console

The R console is where we interact with R. When you see a `>` symbol, that's your prompt to enter commands. In the interactive code blocks below, you'll be able to type and run R code directly.

:::{.callout-tip}
## Pro Tip
Don't worry about making mistakes! Experimentation is a key part of learning. If you get an error, read the message carefully - R usually tells you what went wrong.
:::

## 1. Basic Calculations

R can work as a powerful calculator. Let's try some basic operations:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# Addition
10 + 5

# Subtraction
10 - 5

# Multiplication
10 * 5

# Division
10 / 5

# Exponents (powers)
2 ^ 3

# Integer division
11 %/% 3

# Remainder (modulo)
11 %% 3
```

:::{.callout-note}
## Understanding Operators
- `+` addition
- `-` subtraction
- `*` multiplication
- `/` division
- `^` or `**` exponentiation
- `%/%` integer division
- `%%` modulo (remainder)
:::

## 2. Variables and Assignment

Variables are like containers that store values. In R, we typically use the `<-` operator for assignment:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# Assign a number
fish_count <- 25
fish_count

# Assign text (a string)
species <- "Tuna"
species

# Multiple assignments
length_cm <- 45.5
weight_kg <- 2.3

# Calculate BMI (just as an example)
bmi <- weight_kg / (length_cm/100)^2
bmi
```

:::{.callout-important}
## Naming Rules
- Variable names can contain letters, numbers, dots (.) and underscores (_)
- They must start with a letter or a dot
- R is case-sensitive: `Fish` and `fish` are different variables
- Use descriptive names: `total_catch` is better than `tc`
:::

## 3. Data Types in R

R has several basic data types. Understanding these is crucial:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# Numeric (numbers with decimals)
length_cm <- 45.5
class(length_cm)

# Integer (whole numbers)
fish_count <- 25L  # The L makes it explicitly integer
class(fish_count)

# Character (text)
species <- "Tuna"
class(species)

# Logical (TRUE/FALSE)
is_mature <- TRUE
class(is_mature)

# Check if something is a specific type
is.numeric(length_cm)
is.character(species)
```

## 4. Vectors: Collections of Values

Vectors are one-dimensional arrays that can hold multiple values of the same type:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# Create a numeric vector
fish_lengths <- c(45, 50, 35, 40, 55)

# Create a character vector
species_names <- c("Tuna", "Mackerel", "Sardine")

# Vector operations
mean(fish_lengths)  # Average
max(fish_lengths)   # Maximum value
min(fish_lengths)   # Minimum value
length(fish_lengths)  # Number of elements

# Vector arithmetic
fish_lengths * 2  # Multiply each element by 2

# Accessing elements
fish_lengths[1]  # First element
fish_lengths[2:4]  # Elements 2 to 4
```

:::{.callout-tip}
## Working with Vectors
- Use `c()` to combine values into a vector
- All elements in a vector must be of the same type
- If you mix types, R will convert them to the most flexible type
:::

## 5. Basic Data Frames

Data frames are the most common way to store data in R. Think of them as spreadsheets:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# Create a simple fisheries dataset
fish_data <- data.frame(
  species = c("Tuna", "Mackerel", "Sardine", "Tuna", "Mackerel"),
  length = c(45, 30, 15, 42, 28),
  weight = c(3.5, 1.2, 0.3, 3.2, 1.0)
)

# View the entire data frame
fish_data

# Look at the structure
str(fish_data)

# Basic summary statistics
summary(fish_data)

# Access columns using $
fish_data$length

# Calculate mean length
mean(fish_data$length)

# Filter data
tuna_data <- fish_data[fish_data$species == "Tuna", ]
tuna_data
```

## 6. Basic Plotting

Let's create some simple visualizations of our data:

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# Load ggplot2
library(ggplot2)

# Create a scatter plot
ggplot(fish_data, aes(x = length, y = weight, color = species)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  labs(title = "Fish Length vs Weight by Species",
       x = "Length (cm)",
       y = "Weight (kg)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Practice Exercises 💪

Try these exercises to test your understanding:

1. Create a vector of fish weights: 1.2, 2.3, 3.4, 2.1, 1.9 kg
2. Calculate the average weight
3. Create a new data frame with columns for:
   - date (today's date repeated 3 times)
   - catch (three numbers of your choice)
   - location (three different fishing locations)

Here's the solution - but try it yourself first!

```{webr}
#| autorun: false
# Exercise 1 & 2
weights <- c(1.2, 2.3, 3.4, 2.1, 1.9)
mean(weights)

# Exercise 3
fishing_data <- data.frame(
  date = rep(Sys.Date(), 3),
  catch = c(25, 30, 15),
  location = c("Beach", "Reef", "Harbor")
)
fishing_data
```
